frameworks.name: Acquisition Triangle
frameworks.definition: A three-part framework for guaranteeing employee non-compliance or, inverted, ensuring compliance: (1) Expectation Setting (communication, recording, frequency, metrics), (2) Training (task methodology, prioritization, preferences), (3) Motivation (compensation, purpose, values alignment, self-interest).

claims.text: Employees will not execute expected tasks if you do not communicate the expectation, do not record it in writing, or do not repeat and reinforce it frequently. Silent or one-time verbal requests have near-zero follow-through.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Task expectation communicated only verbally or in passing
No written record of the expectation
No repeated follow-up or metric tracking
claims.mechanism: Absence of recorded clarity and reinforcement signals to the employee that the task has low organizational priority, reducing compliance motivation.
bounded_by: This assumes the employee is otherwise capable and motivated
Does not apply if other structural barriers prevent execution

claims.text: Employees will not execute tasks they are not trained on, even when expectations are clear and communicated. Training gaps occur when: (a) methodology is not taught, (b) time-prioritization relative to workload is not explained, or (c) personal execution preferences are not documented.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Expectation is set and recorded
Employee otherwise has capacity
claims.mechanism: Absence of training creates ambiguity about how to execute and where it fits in competing priorities, causing failure even with good intent.
bounded_by: Assumes the task is teachable and not dependent on unstated tribal knowledge
Does not apply if employee lacks foundational capability for the domain

claims.text: Employee motivation to execute tasks depends on four layers: (1) understanding how the work contributes to organizational outcomes, (2) seeing how it benefits coworkers they care about, (3) recognizing personal self-interest (e.g., higher compensation or bonus eligibility), and (4) alignment with personal values. Absence of any layer reduces motivation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Employee is trained and expectations are clear
Employee is capable of the task
bounded_by: Does not address external demotivation (company instability, leadership distrust)
Assumes the employee has capacity for introspective reflection

claims.text: In conversations addressing non-compliance, beginning with 'it's not like you' reframes the issue as behavioral (not personal), protecting the employee's identity while directly addressing the action gap. This framing enables more receptive problem-solving.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Conversation is one-on-one
Employee has established baseline performance or reputation
Issue is a single uncharacteristic failure or gap
claims.mechanism: Ego protection preserves psychological safety, allowing the employee to admit root cause (knowledge, training, or motivation) without defensiveness.
bounded_by: Does not work for chronic underperformers where non-compliance is characteristic
Requires prior relationship or reputation of competence to be credible

claims.text: The boss's core function is two-fold: (1) train employees on methodology and context, and (2) motivate them by connecting work to outcomes. Hormozi extends this framework by adding a third: ensure the employee even knows the expectation exists in the first place.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Role is managerial or leadership
Goal is systematic employee performance improvement
bounded_by: Does not address firing or exit decisions
Assumes training is feasible (not applicable to roles requiring innate talent)

claims.text: When an employee fails to execute a communicated, trained task, the diagnostic question is: 'Is it that you didn't know [expectation was set], don't know how [to execute], or don't want to [lacking motivation]?' This three-part diagnostic maps to the Acquisition Triangle and guides remediation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Performance gap exists
Expectation, training, and capability have been provisionally ruled in
bounded_by: Assumes the employee will answer truthfully
Does not account for environmental or systemic barriers outside the three categories

claims.text: Direct incentive alignment (e.g., bonus tied to a specific metric like 'fill out sales call notes on 95%+ of calls') increases compliance likelihood substantially compared to relying on purpose or values alone.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Task is measurable and objective
Bonus is meaningful relative to base compensation
Baseline expectations (communication, training) are met

anchors.value: low compliance, reliant on intrinsic motivation

anchors.region: with specific bonus tied to 95%+ completion

bounded_by: Does not apply if the employee cannot afford to fail the metric
Does not address tasks that are difficult to measure objectively

claims.text: Explaining how an employee's task impacts a colleague they care about (e.g., 'Your call notes save Susie in finance 5x effort, enabling her to see her kid') is a powerful motivation lever because it appeals to pro-social values and creates visible causal impact.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Colleague relationship or empathy is likely
Impact is real and quantifiable
Employee has expressed care for work impact on others
claims.mechanism: Pro-social motivation activates when an employee sees their work directly reducing burden on a named individual, converting abstract task into concrete relationship.
bounded_by: Does not work for employees lacking pro-social orientation
Requires that the impact claim is truthful

claims.text: Task explanation should connect work to multiple outcome layers: organizational mission ('this lets us lay the electrical lines'), business outcomes ('you can close higher percentages at higher prices'), and personal economics ('you make more money per hour'). Layered appeals outperform single-lever motivation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Employee has heard the explanation multiple times
The layers are truthful and relevant to the individual
bounded_by: Does not work if any layer is perceived as false
Assumes employee can mentally integrate multiple frames

claims.text: Absence of visible feedback or recognition for completing a task (e.g., not praising work, not showing how it contributed to downstream outcomes) reduces perceived meaningfulness and future compliance motivation, even when the task is otherwise important.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Task is completed
Completion was visible to the manager
No explicit acknowledgment or connection to outcomes was made
claims.mechanism: Lack of feedback creates the perception that the work is pointless ('digging a hole only to push the dirt back in'), removing the reinforcement signal that would strengthen future compliance.
bounded_by: Does not apply if the employee has explicitly stated they do not want feedback
Does not replace other forms of motivation if positive feedback alone is insufficient

examples.text: A sales representative (John) does not fill in call notes after sales calls. The manager explains that without the notes, the finance team member (Susie) must spend overtime manually reconstructing the data, preventing her from being with her children. Additionally, incomplete call notes make it harder for the sales team to close prospects at higher price points. When the manager connects the task to both Susie's overtime burden and John's commission (higher close rates = more commission), and establishes a bonus threshold (95% call note completion), John becomes motivated to comply.

When an employee misses a deadline or fails to execute a communicated task, instead of saying 'You're unreliable,' the manager says 'It's not like you to miss details. Is it that you didn't know this was expected, don't know how to do it, or don't want to?' This three-part diagnostic allows the employee to identify the root cause without feeling personally attacked, making it easier for both to diagnose and fix the actual problem.

practices.text: Record every expectation and task assignment in writing (email, CRM, wiki, or task management system) rather than relying on verbal communication alone.
Repeat expectations and performance metrics frequently (e.g., twice-daily check-ins on critical metrics) to signal organizational priority.
Document personal execution preferences and training methodology so employees know not just what to do but how the manager wants it done.
Train employees on how to prioritize a new task within their existing workload context, not just the task itself.
When recognizing or praising work, explicitly connect it to downstream outcomes ('this is how you lay the electrical lines') to create visible causal impact.
Tie direct financial incentives (bonuses) to specific, measurable task completion thresholds to reinforce compliance.
Ground task explanations in multiple motivation layers: organizational mission, impact on named colleagues, business outcomes, and personal financial benefit.
